# Cardinality of $\mathbb{R}^\infty$

## Setting Up the Problem

The set $\mathbb{R}^\infty$ (also written $\mathbb{R}^{\mathbb{N}}$) is the set of all infinite sequences of real numbers:
$$\mathbb{R}^\infty = \{(a_1, a_2, a_3, \ldots) : a_i \in \mathbb{R}\}.$$

This is the set of all functions $\mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{R}$.

## Computing the Cardinality

Since $|\mathbb{R}| = 2^{\aleph_0}$, we have:

$$|\mathbb{R}^\infty| = |\mathbb{R}|^{|\mathbb{N}|} = \left(2^{\aleph_0}\right)^{\aleph_0}.$$

Using the fundamental law of **cardinal exponentiation** $(\kappa^\lambda)^\mu = \kappa^{\lambda \cdot \mu}$:

$$\left(2^{\aleph_0}\right)^{\aleph_0} = 2^{\aleph_0 \cdot \aleph_0}.$$

Since $\aleph_0 \cdot \aleph_0 = \aleph_0$, this simplifies to:

$$2^{\aleph_0} = \mathfrak{c}.$$

## Comparing with $\beth_1$

The **beth numbers** are defined recursively:
- $\beth_0 = \aleph_0$
- $\beth_1 = 2^{\beth_0} = 2^{\aleph_0}$
- $\beth_2 = 2^{\beth_1} = 2^{2^{\aleph_0}}$
- $\ldots$

Therefore:

$$|\mathbb{R}^\infty| = 2^{\aleph_0} = \beth_1.$$

## Conclusion

Yes, the cardinality of $\mathbb{R}^\infty$ is exactly $\beth_1$.

$$\boxed{\beth_1}$$
